text: Array heap, sift up and sift down.

A binary heap (二叉堆) is a complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i at 2i and 2i + 1, 基础篇第16章) with one rule: every parent ≤ its children. The minimum is always at h[1]. Insert and delete-min each walk one root-to-leaf path: O(log n).
Insert: put the value at the end, then sift up (swap with the parent while smaller). Delete-min: move the last value to the root, then sift down (swap with the smaller child while larger).
The tree has height log₂ n, so sift up and sift down each take O(log n) swaps; reading the minimum is O(1) (P3378). Building a heap from n values by sifting down from n/2 to 1 is even O(n).
priority_queue: two-heap median, k smallest sums, deadlines.

C++ already has a heap: priority_queue<T> keeps the largest on top; priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>> keeps the smallest. push , pop O(log n), top O(1). Pairs compare by the first field, then the second.

Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, with sizes equal or the small half one bigger. The median is then the top of the small half (P1168). The same two-heap split answers "the k- th smallest so far" with a moving k (P1801).

The n smallest of all n² sums: row i is sorted, so only the next unused element of each row can be next; a heap of n "row fronts" gives each answer in O(log n) (P1631, also P2085). Deadlines: take jobs by deadline, and when time runs out drop the longest job taken so far, found in O(log n) with a max-heap (P4053).

Huffman with k-ary trees (P2168) adds zero-weight leaves so that every merge takes exactly k; earthworms (P2827) replace the heap by three queues that stay sorted on their own; dancing pairs (P1878) keep candidate adjacent pairs in a heap and skip stale ones.
lowbit, point update / prefix sum, range add, inversions.

A Fenwick tree (树状数组 , BIT) stores t[i] = sum of a over the block (i − lowbit(i), i], where lowbit(i) = i & −i is the lowest set bit. A prefix sum adds about log n blocks, jumping i −= lowbit(i); a point update changes about log n blocks, jumping i += lowbit(i).
Prefix sums (进阶篇第2章) answer queries in O(1) but cannot change; a Fenwick tree does both query and update in O(log n), with a 10-line implementation.
Point update + range sum (P3374) is the basic form. Store the difference array instead and the same tree does range add + point query (P3368), the 第2章 trick made dynamic.

Inversions again (P1908, also 第3章 by merge sort): scan left to right, and before inserting a[i] ask how many earlier values are ≤ a[i]; the rest of the i earlier values are larger. Discretise first so the values index the tree.

Equal values are not inversions: count earlier values ≤ a[i] (not <), as above. Matching match-sticks (P1966), counting close pairs (P5677) and booking a hall (P2161) all reduce to counting with a Fenwick tree.
